title: How the CRA thinks: self-assessment, audit triggers, documentation
summary: Canada's tax system trusts you to calculate your own tax first, then checks some returns later. Whether you win a review depends far more on the records you kept at the time than on the arguments you make afterwards.
body:
Bottom line. The Canada Revenue Agency, the CRA, lets you calculate your own tax and then reviews a share of returns, sometimes years later. Mr Shabazz, the CRA thinks in documents: if a transaction is not supported by a paper trail made at the time, assume it will be treated as if it did not happen the way you say.

In plain English

Canada uses self-assessment. You, or your company, prepare the return, work out the tax, and pay it. The CRA then issues a notice of assessment, which is its first official statement of what you owe. Often it simply accepts the return at first.

Later, the CRA can reassess, meaning it can change that result, within a time limit called the normal reassessment period. If it finds a problem, it can add tax, interest and in some cases penalties. You can disagree by filing a notice of objection, and later appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

An audit is a review of your records to test the return. It can be a short desk review by letter or a full field audit at your office.

The framework

Understand five ideas about how the CRA approaches a file.

  1. Time limits. Under subsection 152(3.1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), the normal reassessment period is generally three years from the original notice of assessment for individuals and Canadian-controlled private corporations, and four years for other corporations. It can be longer in some cases, such as transactions with non-arm's length non-residents, and has no limit where there is misrepresentation from carelessness or wilful default, or fraud.
  2. Records. Section 230 requires taxpayers carrying on business to keep books and records that allow tax to be determined. As a general rule they must be kept for six years from the end of the last tax year they relate to. Keep them longer when a transaction has a long tail, such as the cost of a property you still own.
  3. Risk selection. The CRA does not publish an exact audit formula. In practice, reviews are more likely for things like large or unusual deductions, losses year after year, related-party transactions, cash-heavy businesses, shareholder loans and benefits, real estate sales that may be business income rather than capital gains, and offshore links. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Burden. In a tax dispute, the CRA's assumptions are generally taken as correct unless you show they are wrong. That makes your own evidence decisive.
  5. Objection deadline. Under subsection 165(1), a notice of objection is generally due within 90 days after the notice of reassessment is sent. Individuals have a longer option in some cases. Miss it and your options shrink sharply.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer's holding company bought a lot for a hypothetical $800,000, held it two years, and sold it for $1,200,000. The company reported a capital gain, where only part of the gain is taxable, rather than business income, which is fully taxable.

Three years later the CRA reviews the sale. Its question is intention: was the lot bought to hold as an investment, or to resell at a profit, which would make the gain business income? The company has three kinds of evidence. A board minute from the purchase date says the lot was bought to build a rental building for long-term income. A rezoning application filed in the first year supports that plan. A lender's term sheet shows long-term rental financing was sought. A later minute records that a change in interest rates made the rental plan unviable, and explains why the company sold.

With that trail, the company can make its case. Without it, the facts look like a quick resale, and a reassessment adding a hypothetical $400,000 of business income becomes far harder to resist.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA) and, if reassessed, tax lawyer

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is writing the explanation after the audit letter arrives. A memo dated after the question is asked carries little weight. The second mistake is ignoring a CRA letter or deadline in the hope that it goes away. Missed deadlines turn an argument you could have won into a debt you must pay.

How you will use it

As a developer, build the habit of the contemporaneous record, meaning a record made at the time of the event. At each purchase, write a short minute saying why the asset is being bought and how it fits the plan. At each change of plan, write down what changed and why. Store contracts, appraisals, lender letters, and invoices in one place for each asset. Keep a log of every related-party payment. Diary the reassessment window for each year's return. When a CRA letter arrives, send it to your advisor the same day and note the response deadline. The CRA reads files, so make sure your file tells the true story without you in the room.
checklist: Write a minute at every purchase stating why the asset is bought
Record every change of plan, with the reason, when it happens
Keep records for at least six years after the last year they relate to
Keep cost records for property as long as you own it, and longer
Log every related-party payment with its purpose
Diary the reassessment window for each tax year
Send any CRA letter to your advisor the same day and note the deadline

selftest.q: Your company sold land two years after buying it and reported a capital gain. The CRA asks why it should not be business income. What evidence would help, and what would not?
selftest.a: Helpful evidence is anything made at the time showing an investment intention: purchase minutes, financing for a long-term hold, rezoning or construction steps, and a dated record of why the plan changed. A memo written after the CRA's question carries little weight. The CRA's assumptions generally stand unless you show they are wrong, so contemporaneous records are decisive.

apply: Pick one asset you own through a company and write a short dated note recording why it was bought and what the plan is today.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): subsection 152(3.1) (normal reassessment period), section 230 (books and records), subsection 165(1) (notice of objection). Audit selection factors are general practice and are tagged unverified. Confirm current text and CRA guidance. Education only, not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA) and, if reassessed, tax lawyer

title: Corporate tax basics: active income, investment income, integration (concepts)
summary: A Canadian private company pays tax at different rates on different kinds of income, and the system tries to make the total tax roughly the same whether income is earned personally or through a company. Knowing which bucket income falls into is the first step in every corporate tax conversation.
body:
Bottom line. A Canadian-controlled private corporation is taxed lightly on active business income it keeps and reinvests, and heavily on investment income, with part of that refunded when dividends are paid. Mr Shabazz, the goal of the system, called integration, is that the total tax ends up roughly similar either way, so a company mainly buys deferral and flexibility, not a permanent discount.

In plain English

A Canadian-controlled private corporation, or CCPC, is a private company controlled by Canadian residents and not by public companies or non-residents. Most owner-managed companies are CCPCs.

Income falls into buckets. Active business income is income from carrying on a real business, such as construction or property development for sale. Investment income, which the Act often calls aggregate investment income, includes interest, most rent from passive holdings, and taxable capital gains. Whether rent is active or passive depends on facts, such as the number of full-time employees. [unverified — confirm independently]

Integration is the design principle that income should bear about the same total tax whether earned directly by a person or earned by a company and then paid out to that person as a dividend.

The framework

These are concepts, and the rates change. Ask your advisor for current numbers.

  1. Small business deduction. Under section 125 of the Income Tax Act (Canada), a CCPC can claim a lower rate on active business income up to a business limit, which is $500,000 a year federally and is shared among associated corporations. Provinces, including Alberta, set their own small business rates and limits.
  2. Associated corporations. Companies controlled by the same person or related people are often associated, so they share one business limit. Splitting a business into many companies does not multiply it.
  3. Passive income grind. The business limit is reduced when a CCPC and its associated corporations earn more than a threshold of adjusted aggregate investment income, set out in subsection 125(5.1). [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Investment income and refundable tax. A CCPC pays a high rate on investment income, including an additional refundable tax under section 123.3. Part of that tax goes into an account called refundable dividend tax on hand and comes back as a dividend refund under section 129 when the company pays taxable dividends.
  5. Two kinds of dividends. Dividends paid out of income taxed at the general rate can be designated eligible dividends and receive a larger dividend tax credit personally. Dividends out of income that used the small business rate are generally non-eligible and receive a smaller credit. The gross-up and credit mechanics are in section 82 and section 121.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical, and the rates are rounded for illustration only. A development company earns a hypothetical $400,000 of active business income from selling finished units. Suppose it pays a combined small business rate of about 11 percent, so about $44,000 of tax. It keeps $356,000 to fund the next project. That is the deferral: money that would have been taxed at a high personal rate stays at work in the company.

Now suppose the company instead parks the cash in term deposits and earns $40,000 of interest. Suppose that interest is taxed at about 47 percent in the company. Much of the refundable part comes back only when the company pays a taxable dividend. If the owner takes that dividend, he pays personal tax on it, and the combined result is designed to land close to what he would have paid earning the interest personally.

The planning lesson: a company is very useful for reinvesting active income, and much less useful for holding passive investments. Large passive balances can also reduce the small business deduction for the operating company.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is believing the company tax rate is the whole story. The low rate is a deferral, not a final rate, because tax is paid again when money comes out as a dividend. The second mistake is splitting operations into many companies to claim many business limits. Association rules generally prevent that.

How you will use it

As a developer, sort each income stream into its bucket before you choose the entity that earns it. Development profit that you will reinvest fits well in an operating company. Long-term rentals may be passive income, depending on the facts, and may belong in a holding company or a different structure. Ask your advisor for a short annual report showing active income, investment income, the refundable tax balance, the dividend accounts and the business limit used across your associated group. Read it before you decide how much to keep in the company and how much to pay out. That one page tells you whether the company is doing what you built it to do. If the numbers surprise you, that is the moment to restructure, not after another year of passive income has built up.
checklist: Confirm each company's status as a Canadian-controlled private corporation
Sort each income stream as active business income or investment income
Map which of your companies are associated and share the business limit
Track investment income across the group against the passive income threshold
Ask for the refundable tax balance and the dividend accounts each year
Treat the low corporate rate as deferral, not a final rate
Decide where long-term rentals should sit with advice on the facts

selftest.q: You hold five operating companies, each owned by you, and plan to claim the full small business limit in each. Your company also holds a large term deposit portfolio. What two problems might your advisor raise?
selftest.a: First, the five companies are likely associated, so they share one business limit rather than each getting their own. Second, large investment income in the associated group can reduce that shared business limit under the passive income rules, raising tax on the active income.

apply: List each income stream your companies earn and label it active, investment, or unsure. Take the unsure items to your advisor.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 125 (small business deduction and $500,000 business limit), subsection 125(5.1) (business limit reduction; threshold tagged unverified), section 123.3 (refundable tax), section 129 (dividend refund), sections 82 and 121 (gross-up and dividend tax credit). The active or passive treatment of rent and all rates in the example are tagged unverified or hypothetical. Education only, not tax advice.

title: Personal vs corporate: salary, dividends, shareholder loans and benefits
summary: An owner can take money out of a company as salary, as dividends, as a loan or as a benefit, and the tax result is different for each. Shareholder loans and personal use of company assets are the routes most likely to cause tax trouble.
body:
Bottom line. There are four ways money leaves a company for its owner: salary, dividends, loans and benefits. Mr Shabazz, salary and dividends are the planned routes; loans and personal use of company assets are where most owners get hurt, because the tax law can turn them into income without warning.

In plain English

Salary, or wages, is payment for work. The company deducts it as an expense, and the owner pays personal tax on it. Dividends are a share of after-tax profit paid to shareholders. The company cannot deduct them, but the owner gets a dividend tax credit to reflect the tax the company already paid.

A shareholder loan is money the company lends to a shareholder or a person connected to one. A shareholder benefit is any value the owner gets from the company without paying for it, such as personal use of a company vehicle or the company paying a personal bill.

The framework

  1. Salary. Deductible to the company if reasonable. Taxable to the owner. It creates contribution room for a registered retirement savings plan and requires Canada Pension Plan contributions and payroll remittances. It needs payroll accounts, source deductions sent to the CRA on time, and T4 slips.
  2. Dividends. Paid from after-tax profit and declared by a directors' resolution. No payroll, no pension contributions, no retirement savings room. The tax on split income rules in section 120.4 of the Income Tax Act (Canada) can tax dividends paid to family members at the top rate unless an exclusion applies.
  3. Shareholder loans. Under subsection 15(2), a loan from a company to a shareholder or connected person can be included in the borrower's income. A key exception applies if the loan is repaid within one year after the end of the company's tax year in which it was made, and the repayment is not part of a series of loans and repayments. There are other narrow exceptions. Even when a loan is not included, section 80.4 can deem a taxable benefit for interest at the prescribed rate if the loan carries a lower rate.
  4. Benefits. Under subsection 15(1), the value of a benefit conferred on a shareholder is generally included in the shareholder's income, while the company usually cannot deduct the cost. That is taxed twice in effect.
  5. Reasonableness. Section 67 limits deductions to amounts that are reasonable. Large salaries to family members who do little work can be challenged.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer's company has a year end of December 31. In March of year 1, he takes a hypothetical $150,000 from the company to pay for a personal home renovation, recorded as a loan on the books.

To avoid inclusion under subsection 15(2), the loan generally must be repaid by December 31 of year 2, one year after the end of year 1. In December of year 2, he repays it by declaring a $150,000 bonus, paying the tax on the bonus, and applying the net amount plus personal cash to the loan. The repayment is real and is not followed by a fresh loan in January.

If instead he repays the loan on December 30 of year 2 and borrows it back on January 2 of year 3, the CRA may treat this as a series of loans and repayments, include the amount in his income anyway, and assess interest. And during the time the loan was outstanding, if no interest was charged, a deemed interest benefit may apply.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is treating the company bank account as a personal wallet and sorting it out at year end. Personal expenses paid by the company become either a shareholder loan, with a deadline, or a benefit, with double tax. The second mistake is paying family members salaries or dividends without checking reasonableness and tax on split income first.

How you will use it

As a developer, decide each year, before the year starts, how you will be paid: a planned mix of salary and dividends, chosen with your advisor based on retirement savings goals, pension contributions, the company's cash needs and family circumstances. Pay personal costs personally. If you must borrow from the company, sign a loan agreement, set interest at or above the prescribed rate, and diary the repayment deadline. Keep a running shareholder loan account and review it every quarter, not once a year. Company vehicles and property used personally need a written policy and a calculated benefit. These habits keep money moving out of the company on purpose, rather than by accident. When a lender asks for your personal income, the planned salary and dividend record also helps, because it shows steady, documented income rather than irregular draws. And if a dispute ever arises with a partner or a buyer, a clean shareholder loan account is one of the first things their accountant will check. It is easier to keep it clean than to explain it later.
checklist: Set the year's salary and dividend mix with your advisor before the year starts
Run payroll properly for any salary, with source deductions remitted on time
Declare dividends by directors' resolution and record them in the minute book
Check tax on split income before paying any family member a dividend
Pay personal costs personally, not from the company account
Document any shareholder loan, charge interest, and diary the repayment date
Review the shareholder loan account every quarter

selftest.q: Your company's year end is June 30. On August 1 of year 1 you take a hypothetical $60,000 personal loan from it. By what date must it generally be repaid to avoid inclusion under subsection 15(2), and what else should you watch?
selftest.a: The tax year in which the loan was made ends June 30 of year 2, so it must generally be repaid by June 30 of year 3, one year after that year end. The repayment must not be part of a series of loans and repayments, and a deemed interest benefit under section 80.4 may apply while the loan is outstanding if no interest or low interest is charged.

apply: Ask your bookkeeper for the current balance of every shareholder loan account and the date each balance arose.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): subsection 15(1) (shareholder benefits), subsection 15(2) and related rules (shareholder loans and the one-year repayment exception), section 80.4 (deemed interest), section 67 (reasonableness), section 120.4 (tax on split income). Confirm current text and the prescribed rate with the CRA. Education only, not tax advice.

title: Compliance calendar: filings, elections and the cost of being late
summary: Every company, trust and owner has fixed filing and payment dates, and missing them costs penalties and interest even when no extra tax is owed. Some elections can only be made by a deadline, so a missed date can cost a tax result permanently.
body:
Bottom line. Tax compliance is a calendar, not a task you do when you have time. Mr Shabazz, late filing creates penalties and interest automatically, and a missed election deadline can cost a tax deferral you planned for years, so put every date in one calendar with reminders well ahead.

In plain English

A filing deadline is the last day to send a return. A payment deadline is the last day to pay the tax, and it is often earlier than the filing deadline. Instalments are advance payments of tax made during the year. An election is a formal choice, made on a prescribed form, that changes how the tax law treats a transaction. Many elections must be filed by a set date.

The framework

These are the main federal dates for an owner-managed group. Confirm the current rules, because some have conditions.

  1. Corporate return. Under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), a corporation's T2 return is due within six months after its tax year ends. Alberta corporations also file an Alberta corporate return, because Alberta administers its own corporate income tax. [unverified — confirm independently]
  2. Corporate tax payment. The balance of corporate tax is generally due two months after year end, or three months for certain Canadian-controlled private corporations that meet conditions about the small business deduction and size. [unverified — confirm independently]
  3. Corporate instalments. Section 157 generally requires monthly instalments, or quarterly for certain small CCPCs.
  4. Personal return. An individual's return is generally due April 30, or June 15 if the individual or spouse carried on a business, but any balance owing is still due April 30.
  5. Trust return. A trust's T3 return is generally due within 90 days after its tax year ends, under paragraph 150(1)(c). Most personal trusts have a December 31 year end.
  6. Payroll and slips. Source deductions are remitted on a schedule set by the size of the payroll. T4 and T5 slips are generally due by the end of February. [unverified — confirm independently]
  7. GST/HST. Registrants file on a monthly, quarterly or annual schedule, and sales of new housing or commercial property have their own rules.
  8. Corporate registry. Each company must file an annual return with the provincial or federal registry to stay in good standing. A company struck off for not filing may lose the power to act until revived. [unverified — confirm independently]

Now the cost of being late. Under subsection 162(1), the penalty for a late return is 5 percent of the unpaid tax plus 1 percent of the unpaid tax for each full month late, up to 12 months. Subsection 162(2) sets a higher penalty for repeat failures. Interest on unpaid tax and late instalments is charged under section 161 at the prescribed rate, compounded daily, and is not deductible.

Elections need their own column. A rollover of property to a corporation under section 85 needs a joint election, usually on form T2057, filed by the deadline set in the section. Late filing is possible in some cases with a penalty, and beyond a point only with the CRA's permission. Many other elections have similar deadlines. [unverified — confirm independently]

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A holding company has a December 31 year end and owes a hypothetical $50,000 of tax for year 1. Its return is due June 30 of year 2, but the payment was due at the end of February or March of year 2. The bookkeeper is late, and the return is filed in early October, three full months late.

The late filing penalty is 5 percent of $50,000, which is $2,500, plus 1 percent a month for three months, which is $1,500, for a total of $4,000. Interest runs on the $50,000 from the payment due date, at the prescribed rate, until it is paid. None of it is deductible. Had the payment been made on time, the late filing penalty would have been based on zero unpaid tax.

Now add a missed election. The company also received land from its owner in year 1, intending a section 85 rollover at cost. If the election is not filed, the transfer may be treated as made at fair market value, triggering the full gain.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (CPA)

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is assuming the filing deadline is also the payment deadline. Corporate tax is often due months before the return. The second mistake is assuming an accountant tracks every election automatically. Elections tied to transactions in the year, such as a rollover, must be flagged when the transaction happens.

How you will use it

As a developer, keep one compliance calendar for every entity you own or control: companies, trusts and yourself. List each year end, filing date, payment date, instalment dates, payroll remittance dates, GST/HST dates and the registry annual return. Add every election triggered by a transaction the day the deal closes. Set reminders 60 and 30 days before each date, and ask your bookkeeper to confirm in writing when each item is done. Pay the tax by the payment date even if the return is not ready; that alone removes most of the late filing penalty. A calendar like this costs an hour to build and saves real money every year.
checklist: List every entity you control with its year end
Record the filing date and the separate payment date for each
Add instalment, payroll, GST/HST and registry annual return dates
Add each election the day the transaction that triggers it closes
Set reminders 60 and 30 days ahead
Pay tax by the payment date even if the return is late
Get written confirmation when each filing is done

selftest.q: Your company owes a hypothetical $20,000 for a year and the return is filed five full months late. What is the late filing penalty, and how could you have avoided most of it even with the late return?
selftest.a: The penalty is 5 percent of $20,000, which is $1,000, plus 1 percent a month for five months, which is $1,000, for $2,000 in total, plus interest. Because the penalty is based on unpaid tax, paying the tax by the payment due date would have reduced the penalty base to zero, leaving little or no late filing penalty.

apply: Build a one-page compliance calendar listing every entity you control, its year end, filing date and payment date.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): paragraphs 150(1)(a) and 150(1)(c) (filing dates), section 157 (instalments), subsections 162(1) and 162(2) (late filing penalties), section 161 (interest), section 85 (rollover election). Balance-due dates, slip dates, the Alberta corporate return and registry annual returns are tagged unverified; confirm with the CRA, Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, and the corporate registry. Education only, not tax advice.
